title: LIMIT
description: Use MySQL LIMIT with filtering and deterministic ordering; understand tied boundaries, short results, input validation, and query-cost limits.
notes:
## A row cap answers how many, not which ones

LIMIT places an upper bound on the number of rows returned by a MySQL query. A campus equipment list may show the first three available items or display a short recent-request panel. The cap controls output size, but another rule must define which qualifying items deserve those positions. Keep eligibility, ordering and row count as separate decisions in the query contract.

A limit without ordering can still be useful when any small subset is acceptable for inspection. It is not inherently meaningless or invalid. It simply does not promise the cheapest, newest or same identities on repeated runs. State whether the feature accepts an arbitrary subset or requires a defined ordered selection so consumers do not infer a ranking that the query never expressed.

## The cap is a maximum rather than a target

If a query qualifies eight rows and requests a limit of one thousand, it returns the eight available rows rather than padding the result or raising an error for the unused capacity. If no rows qualify, the result is empty. The limit does not manufacture equipment or repeat existing rows to reach a requested page size.

LIMIT zero requests no result rows. That is different from omitting a limit or using an application convention in which zero means unlimited. Validate the endpoint's own interpretation before constructing SQL. A UI displaying no items might reflect a zero-sized request, an empty qualifying population or another application state; the database cap alone does not classify all those possibilities.

## Ordering defines the selected prefix

The cheapest three items require an ascending price order. The newest three requests require a suitable timestamp order, usually descending. The database does not infer either ranking from LIMIT. An identity can be a reliable tie breaker without necessarily being a trustworthy proxy for time, especially when identifiers are imported, generated by another system or assigned before an event is finalized.

```sql
SELECT equipment_id, price
FROM equipment_prices
ORDER BY price ASC, equipment_id ASC
LIMIT 3;
```

The result is the first at-most-three rows of that specified sequence. A complete order is particularly important when the cap cuts through a group of equal prices. Without a final distinguishing key, several different subsets can satisfy the same price order. The query remains price ordered while failing a consumer's stronger expectation of fixed identity membership.

## Exactly a count and all rank ties differ

A feature asking for exactly three qualifying identities chooses a policy for equal values at the boundary. A feature asking for all items tied at the third-ranked price can return more than three identities. Ordinary LIMIT three does not automatically include every tie. Write and explain the intended rank or boundary-value logic when that broader tie-preserving result is required.

The beginner exercise chooses at most three rows with an explicit identity tie breaker. That gives a deterministic subset under its fixed input. It does not assert that every equally priced item belongs in the output. A tie fixture with more than three cheap items shows which interpretation the task uses and prevents a solution from relying on arbitrary physical retrieval order.

## Filter before applying the requested row cap

When the requirement asks for the newest active requests, the qualifying active population needs to be defined before its ordered prefix is selected. Taking several newest requests regardless of status and filtering them later can return too few active items even when more qualifying active requests exist. The location of the cap in composed queries changes the question being answered.

The logical result is easiest to explain as eligible rows, then their sequence, then the admitted prefix. Physical execution can optimize that work without changing the answer. Do not assume the database must materialize every logical stage or that the cap always prevents it from inspecting excluded candidates. Eligibility and ranking conditions determine what work is actually necessary.

## A limit belongs to a query scope

An inner query's cap can select one intermediate population, while an outer query can further join, filter or order those rows. That composition does not automatically implement the same requirement as a single final cap after all relationships are evaluated. A join can multiply a limited set of equipment rows into many result rows, changing both output count and grain.

Decide whether the cap applies to equipment identities, checkout events or final displayed rows. If the report needs three equipment items with their full tag lists, limiting joined tag rows can truncate one item's detail and exclude another item unexpectedly. Choose the query shape around the required grain rather than place LIMIT wherever it is most convenient to type.

## Known and missing ranking values need a policy

A nullable timestamp or price can affect which rows enter the limited prefix. MySQL's default ascending order places [NULL](/learning/dbms-sql-tutorial/null-values) before known values. If a cheapest-items panel should include priced equipment first, explicitly define missing-price placement or eligibility. A cap does not make an unknown price into a known cheap value merely because it appears early in the default order.

For newest-event lists, a missing event time might be excluded, placed last or surfaced in a separate investigation panel. The intermediate exercise requires a known timestamp and an active status, then orders by newest timestamp and descending identity. That contract avoids guessing how a pending unknown time should compete with accepted known events.

## Small output does not guarantee small work

A suitable index and selective predicate can help an engine find an ordered prefix efficiently. A different query may inspect many rows, perform joins or sort a large qualifying population before returning a few rows. LIMIT controls the result size, not a universal upper bound on scanned rows, memory or execution time. Measure representative plans when performance matters.

Avoid removing necessary filters or tie breakers to obtain a superficially cheaper plan. A fast arbitrary subset does not satisfy a newest-active-request contract. Bound expensive user-controlled search input and retrieval sizes at the application boundary, but retain the data-access rules that define permitted results. Output optimization cannot replace correctness or authorization.

## Validate requested sizes at the trusted boundary

An API receiving a page size should require an appropriate integer range and enforce a reasonable feature-specific maximum. Use the database client's supported binding or query-construction mechanism rather than concatenate untrusted syntax. A negative or malformed size should not silently become a broad unrestricted request. The application contract should define rejected values and any explicit default.

The cap also is not an access policy. A query returning only one private row is still a disclosure if the caller lacks permission. Enforce trusted row access independently, then apply the consumer's requested cap within that permitted scope. UI controls that offer only small sizes do not establish what a caller can request directly.

## Limited pages observe changing data

A complete order defines a deterministic prefix for a given visible dataset. Between requests, new rows can enter that prefix or updated values can move existing rows. A recent-items panel may intentionally reflect live changes, while an export may require a consistent snapshot. LIMIT does not freeze the underlying data or provide a universal consistency policy for later pages.

If the interface needs continuation, design its [offset](/learning/dbms-sql-tutorial/offset) or keyset rule using the same ordering contract. A first-page cap is only the starting point of that design. Preserve the distinction between a stable sequence within one observation and stable membership over time so tests do not claim concurrency guarantees from one static fixture.

## Test fewer rows, ties and excluded near misses

The first exercise returns the cheapest three known-price rows with identity ties, including a fixture containing fewer than three rows. The second returns the two newest active requests with known timestamps. Its alternatives include newer inactive requests and equal-time active requests, exposing a missing status filter or omitted tie breaker.

Explain the qualifying population before listing the admitted identities. Then show how the ordering and cap together choose that prefix. An empty result and a short result are valid when the data supports them; neither should be patched by relaxing the requirement. A clear bounded query names what qualifies, how it ranks and the maximum number the consumer is entitled to receive.

questions.question_text: What does LIMIT specify in a MySQL SELECT?
options: A maximum number of returned rows
questions.explanation: It bounds output without defining eligibility or ranking.

questions.question_text: Without ORDER BY, does LIMIT 3 guarantee the same three identities in the same sequence?
options: Only if the table is small
questions.explanation: An arbitrary observed access order is not a ranking contract.

questions.question_text: Can an unordered LIMIT be useful when any small subset is acceptable?
questions.explanation: It is insufficient for a specific ordered-selection requirement, not universally useless.

questions.question_text: Eight rows qualify and LIMIT 1000 is requested. What is returned?
questions.explanation: The cap is an upper bound.

questions.question_text: What is missing from a query intended to show newest requests using only LIMIT 10?
options: An explicit appropriate time order and tie policy
A requirement to return all statuses
questions.explanation: The cap does not infer newest.

questions.question_text: What does LIMIT 0 return?
questions.explanation: Application-specific zero conventions must not be confused with SQL.

questions.question_text: Which form selects the cheapest five under a complete known-price order?
options: ORDER BY price ASC,id ASC LIMIT 5
questions.explanation: Ranking and identity ties define the selected prefix.

questions.question_text: What should be verified before moving a LIMIT query to another SQL engine?
options: That engine’s supported bounded-result syntax and semantics
That every engine uses identical syntax
That the table has no keys
questions.explanation: The package uses MySQL forms.

questions.question_text: Does ordinary LIMIT 3 include all rows tied at the third price?
questions.explanation: An all-rank-ties contract needs different explicit logic.

questions.question_text: Why is an id not automatically the same as event recency?
options: Generation or import policy can differ from event time
questions.explanation: Use the authoritative recency property.

questions.question_text: What is the intended logical population for newest active requests?
options: A capped arbitrary population filtered later
Active eligible rows ordered newest first, then capped
Only rows with the smallest id
questions.explanation: Premature limiting can change the answer.

questions.question_text: Why can limiting joined rows fail a three-equipment-with-all-tags report?
options: Joins always return one row per equipment
One equipment can occupy several joined rows and be truncated
questions.explanation: Define the cap at the required result grain.

questions.question_text: What can missing prices do under MySQL default ascending order?
options: Appear before known prices and enter the limited prefix
questions.explanation: Specify missingness placement or eligibility deliberately.

questions.question_text: Does LIMIT 5 prove that at most five candidates were examined?
questions.explanation: Result size is not a work bound.

questions.question_text: How should an API treat an invalid negative page size?
options: Use its explicit validation and rejection contract
Treat it as permission to read everything
questions.explanation: Trusted construction should not broaden malformed requests.

questions.question_text: Can returning only one row still disclose unauthorized information?
options: No, one row is always safe
Only if the query has no limit
Only if the row is old
questions.explanation: Access checks are independent of output count.

questions.question_text: Does LIMIT freeze the same visible prefix across later requests?
options: No, changed data can change membership
questions.explanation: Consistency and continuation require their own design.

questions.question_text: Which fixture exposes an omitted active-status filter?
options: A newer inactive request that should not qualify
questions.explanation: Near misses distinguish required eligibility.

questions.question_text: Which fixture tests the cap’s maximum rather than exact-count nature?
options: Fewer qualifying rows than the limit
questions.explanation: The short result remains valid.

questions.question_text: What should a bounded-query explanation identify?
options: Eligibility, complete ordering and maximum count
questions.explanation: Those three decisions jointly define the requested prefix.

coding_problems.title: Select at most three cheapest equipment rows
coding_problems.task: Return equipment_id,price for at most three rows with the smallest price, resolving equal prices by equipment_id ascending. All prices are known. Preserve all source rows.
coding_problems.schema_sql: CREATE TABLE equipment_prices(equipment_id INT PRIMARY KEY,price INT NOT NULL);
coding_problems.ordering: As explicitly ordered in the result query.
constraints: Use only the supplied synthetic tables and requested transition.
edge_cases: Fewer than three available rows produce a short result.
A tie at the cap uses identity.
hints: Define the complete order before the cap.
Do not expand the output to all tied rows.
coding_problems.solution_sql: SELECT equipment_id,price FROM equipment_prices ORDER BY price ASC,equipment_id ASC LIMIT 3;
coding_problems.explanation: The full sequence ranks price then identity; the cap admits its first three rows rather than every price tie.

coding_problems.title: Return two newest dated active requests
coding_problems.task: Return request_id,created_at for at most two rows with status='active' and known created_at. Sort created_at descending, then request_id descending for equal times. Preserve source data.
coding_problems.schema_sql: CREATE TABLE requests(request_id INT PRIMARY KEY,status VARCHAR(20) NOT NULL,created_at DATETIME);
coding_problems.ordering: As explicitly ordered in the result query.
constraints: Use only the supplied synthetic tables and requested transition.
edge_cases: A newer closed row must not displace an active row.
An unknown timestamp is excluded by contract.
hints: Filter status and timestamp presence explicitly.
Use both descending ordering keys before LIMIT.
coding_problems.solution_sql: SELECT request_id,created_at FROM requests WHERE status='active' AND created_at IS NOT NULL ORDER BY created_at DESC,request_id DESC LIMIT 2;
coding_problems.explanation: Eligibility excludes closed and undated rows before the requested ordered prefix. Descending identity supplies the specified equal-time order.

original_questions.question_text: What does the LIMIT clause do?
options: Filters rows matching a WHERE condition
Restricts the maximum number of rows returned by the query
Groups rows into batches of a fixed size
original_questions.explanation: LIMIT caps the row count of the result set; it does not filter, group, or sort on its own.

original_questions.question_text: What is guaranteed about the result of `SELECT name FROM products LIMIT 3;` with no ORDER BY, run twice on the same unchanged table?
options: It always returns the 3 most recently inserted rows
It always returns the same 3 rows in the same order both times
Nothing is guaranteed — the engine may return different rows or a different order between runs
It always returns rows in primary key order
original_questions.explanation: Without ORDER BY, LIMIT's chosen rows depend on the query plan and storage details, which are not guaranteed to be stable or repeatable.

original_questions.question_text: Why is `LIMIT` considered meaningless on its own, without ORDER BY?
options: Because LIMIT is deprecated in modern SQL
Because it always returns zero rows unless ORDER BY is present
Because which specific rows get returned is undefined without a sort order, so the result is not reproducible
Because LIMIT requires a WHERE clause to function
original_questions.explanation: LIMIT simply cuts off the result stream at N rows; without ORDER BY there's no defined stream to cut, so the chosen rows are arbitrary.

original_questions.question_text: What happens if you request `LIMIT 1000` but the query only matches 8 rows?
options: An error is raised for requesting more rows than exist
All 8 matching rows are returned with no error
Exactly 1000 rows are returned, padded with NULLs
The query silently returns zero rows
original_questions.explanation: LIMIT never pads or errors; it simply returns as many rows as are available, up to the requested cap.

original_questions.question_text: A developer writes `SELECT * FROM orders LIMIT 10;` intending to always show the 10 newest orders. What is wrong with this query?
options: Nothing — LIMIT always returns the most recently inserted rows by default
It needs an ORDER BY (e.g. by created_at DESC) because LIMIT alone does not guarantee 'newest' or any particular order
LIMIT can only be used with UPDATE statements, not SELECT
It should use OFFSET instead of LIMIT
original_questions.explanation: LIMIT has no inherent notion of 'newest'; without an explicit ORDER BY on a relevant column, the returned rows are arbitrary.
LIMIT 0 explicitly requests zero rows, sometimes used to check query validity without fetching data.

original_questions.question_text: Which query below is guaranteed to deterministically return the 5 cheapest products every time it runs (assuming price is unique)?
options: SELECT name, price FROM products LIMIT 5;
SELECT name, price FROM products ORDER BY price ASC LIMIT 5;
SELECT name, price FROM products WHERE price > 0 LIMIT 5;
SELECT TOP 5 name, price FROM products;  -- with no ORDER BY equivalent logic
original_questions.explanation: Only pairing LIMIT with an explicit ORDER BY on price guarantees which specific rows and in what order are returned.

original_questions.question_text: In SQL Server, which construct is the rough equivalent of PostgreSQL/MySQL's LIMIT?
original_questions.explanation: SQL Server uses TOP n (or the standard FETCH FIRST n ROWS ONLY) instead of the LIMIT keyword used by PostgreSQL, MySQL, and SQLite.
